title: Why can a transaction still roll back even after you catch the exception? What is the difference between logical and physical transaction scope?
keyPoints: REQUIRED propagation means inner and outer methods share one physical transaction
When the inner method throws RuntimeException, the proxy marks the shared physical TX as rollback-only
The rollback-only flag cannot be cleared once set -- the transaction is doomed
If the outer method catches the exception and tries to commit, Spring throws UnexpectedRollbackException
The distinction is logical vs physical scope: each method has a logical TX, but they share one physical TX
Fix: use REQUIRES_NEW on the inner method so it runs in its own physical transaction
Alternative fix: do not make the inner method @Transactional if it does not need its own TX behavior

s1_definition.oneliner: UnexpectedRollbackException occurs when an inner REQUIRED method marks the shared physical transaction as rollback-only, and the outer method catches the exception and tries to commit -- the commit fails because the transaction is already doomed.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Logical transaction** -- each `@Transactional` method has its own logical transaction scope. It thinks it has its own transaction, but with REQUIRED propagation, it shares the physical one.
- **Physical transaction** -- the actual database transaction backed by a single JDBC connection. With REQUIRED, all methods in the call chain share one physical transaction.
- **Rollback-only flag** -- when the inner method throws a RuntimeException, the proxy calls `setRollbackOnly()` on the shared physical transaction. This flag cannot be cleared.
- **UnexpectedRollbackException** -- when the outer method catches the exception and its proxy tries to commit, Spring sees the rollback-only flag, rolls back, and throws this exception to signal that the requested commit was refused.
- **Fix with REQUIRES_NEW** -- give the inner method its own physical transaction so its failure does not poison the outer one.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, two officers share one vault session (physical transaction). The junior officer (inner method) makes a mistake and stamps the vault log "CANCEL ALL" (rollback-only). The senior officer (outer method) catches the mistake and tries to continue, but when they try to close the vault (commit), the vault refuses because the log says "CANCEL ALL." The senior is surprised: the error was caught, but the vault session was already poisoned.

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  REQUIRED: shared physical TX                             │
│                                                           │
│  Outer Method (TX-1)          Inner Method (joins TX-1)  │
│  ──────────────────          ──────────────────────────   │

│  credit CUR3001               validate()                 │
│          │                        │                       │

│          │               proxy calls setRollbackOnly()    │
│          │                        │                       │

│     (thinks it recovered)                                 │
│          │                                                │
│     return normally                                       │
│          │                                                │
│     proxy tries COMMIT                                    │
│          │                                                │
│     sees rollback-only flag                               │
│          │                                                │
│     ROLLBACK TX-1                                         │
│          │                                                │
│     throws UnexpectedRollbackException                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  REQUIRES_NEW: separate physical TXs                      │
│                                                           │
│  Outer Method (TX-1)          Inner Method (TX-2)        │
│  ──────────────────          ────────────────────         │
│  BEGIN TX-1                                               │
│  debit SAV2001                                            │
│  credit CUR3001               BEGIN TX-2                 │
│          │                    validate()                  │
│     TX-1 SUSPENDED            throws RuntimeException     │
│          │                    ROLLBACK TX-2               │
│     TX-1 RESUMED                                          │
│     catch(e) { ... }                                      │
│          │                                                │
│     return normally                                       │
│          │                                                │
│     proxy COMMITS TX-1 -> SUCCESS                         │
│     (TX-1 was never poisoned)                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
UnexpectedRollbackException occurs when an inner @Transactional method with REQUIRED propagation throws a RuntimeException. The proxy around the inner method marks the shared physical transaction as rollback-only, and this flag cannot be cleared. Even if the outer method catches the exception and tries to continue, the commit fails because the physical transaction is doomed. The distinction is between logical and physical transaction scope: both methods logically think they have their own transaction, but REQUIRED means they share one physical transaction, and the inner failure contaminates it.

In Rajesh's batch payment service at the National Bank of India, processing three payments in one transaction with a REQUIRED inner validator means one invalid payment poisons the entire batch. All three payments are lost, including the valid ones. The fix is using REQUIRES_NEW on the validator so each validation runs in its own physical transaction. If validation fails, only the inner transaction rolls back, and the outer transaction is unaffected.

The simpler alternative is to not make the validator @Transactional at all. If the validator is a plain method that throws an exception, no proxy is involved, and no rollback-only flag is set. The outer method can catch the exception and continue without any transaction infrastructure interference.

Remember one sentence: REQUIRED means one physical transaction for all participants, so an inner failure poisons the whole chain -- use REQUIRES_NEW or remove @Transactional from the inner method to isolate failures.
